The guidelines include detailed recommendations on hepatitis B and C testing strategies, diagnostic accuracy, and cost-effectiveness. For hepatitis B, testing strategies focus on detecting hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) using one-assay or two-assay approaches. For hepatitis C, testing strategies include anti-HCV testing and nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HCV RNA to confirm active infection. The use of dried blood spots (DBS) as a sample collection method for serology and NAT is also evaluated. The guidelines emphasize the importance of monitoring treatment response in individuals with confirmed active HCV infection, comparing HCV core antigen testing with NAT for HCV RNA detection. Monitoring for treatment response and adherence is recommended, particularly in individuals with advanced liver disease or HIV co-infection. For hepatitis B, non-invasive tests such as the aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index (APRI) are recommended to assess liver disease stage, especially in resource-limited settings. FibroScan or FibroTest may be preferred where available and affordable. Treatment is prioritized for individuals with clinical evidence of cirrhosis, regardless of ALT levels, HBeAg status, or HBV DNA levels. In the absence of HBV DNA testing, treatment may be considered based on persistently abnormal ALT levels alone. For individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) who do not meet treatment criteria, continued monitoring is essential to determine if antiviral therapy may be needed in the future to prevent progressive liver disease. Monitoring should include ALT, AST, HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA levels (if available), as well as non-invasive tests for cirrhosis. More frequent monitoring is recommended for individuals with fluctuating ALT or HBV DNA levels, those with HIV co-infection, or those on treatment. Routine surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with abdominal ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein testing every six months is recommended for individuals with cirrhosis, a family history of HCC, or those aged over 40 years with high HBV DNA levels. The guidelines also address the importance of monitoring for tenofovir and entecavir toxicity, including baseline and annual renal function assessments, and careful growth monitoring in children.
